records.title: Water Leak at Rear Window/Third Brake Light
records.description: Water can leak into the cabin through the rear window seal or third brake light area, causing wet carpets in the rear and potential electrical issues. The sliding rear window models seem more susceptible to leaks.
records.solution: Inspect rear window seal and third brake light seal for gaps or deterioration. Apply additional sealant around third brake light. Have dealer reseal rear window if needed. Check drain holes in bed area are not clogged.
symptoms: Wet carpet in rear of cab
Water on rear seats after rain
Musty smell in cabin
Water dripping from headliner
Fog or condensation in third brake light

records.title: Excessive Wind Noise from Doors/Windows
records.description: Many Ranger owners report excessive wind noise at highway speeds, particularly around the front door seals, mirrors, and A-pillars. This can make highway driving fatiguing and affect audio clarity. Door seal alignment issues are often the culprit.
records.solution: Have dealer inspect and adjust door seals and alignment. Apply additional weather stripping if needed. Some owners have had door seals replaced under warranty. Aftermarket mirror caps or wind deflectors may help reduce turbulence.
symptoms: Loud wind noise at highway speeds
Whistling from door area
Noise from mirror area
Wind noise increases with speed
Difficulty hearing audio at highway speeds

records.title: 6.7L Power Stroke CP4 High-Pressure Fuel Pump Failure - Catastrophic Fuel System Contamination
records.description: The 2011-2016 6.7L Power Stroke uses a Bosch CP4.2 high-pressure fuel injection pump that is fundamentally incompatible with North American diesel fuel specifications. US diesel fuel has lower lubricity than European fuel, and the CP4 pump relies on fuel for internal lubrication. Over time, the CP4 pump's internal metal components grind and generate metal shavings that are distributed throughout the entire high-pressure fuel system at 30,000+ PSI. Metal contamination destroys all downstream injectors, fuel rails, and low-pressure system components. A class action lawsuit filed against Ford alleges the company knew the CP4 was incompatible with US fuel. Catastrophic failure can occur as early as 80,000-120,000 miles and requires complete fuel system replacement costing $8,000-$15,000.
records.solution: Complete fuel system replacement required: CP4 pump, all 8 injectors, high-pressure fuel rails, low-pressure pump, fuel filter housing, all fuel lines (metal contamination spreads everywhere). Ford kit EC3Z-9B246-C covers the repair for some years. Total cost $8,000-$15,000. Prevention: add diesel fuel lubricity additive (Stanadyne Performance Formula, Hot Shots Secret DIESEL EXTREME) at every fill-up. Some owners install a CP3 conversion pump kit (eliminates the CP4 with a more reliable Bosch CP3).
symptoms: Loss of power during acceleration
Engine hesitation and stumbling under load
Hard start or no-start condition
Smoke from exhaust (black or white)
Check engine light with fuel system pressure codes
Loud ticking or knocking from injector area
Fuel rail pressure too low codes (P0087, P0191)
Complete engine shutdown on the road

records.title: 6.7L Power Stroke DEF/SCR System Failure - P207F and P20EE Codes
records.description: The Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) system on 2015-2022 6.7L Power Stroke trucks - which uses Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) to reduce NOx emissions - is prone to failure, most commonly triggering DTC codes P207F (Reductant Quality Performance) and P20EE (SCR NOx Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold). Causes include degraded or crystallized DEF fluid (DEF has a shelf life of 1-2 years and degrades faster in heat), a failed DEF injector, SCR catalyst failure, DEF quality sensor failure, or NOx sensor failure. In limp mode, the truck's performance is severely limited. The system is complex and diagnosis requires a professional scan tool. The DEF injector is a particularly common failure point on 2017+ trucks.
records.solution: Diagnose with Ford IDS or quality OBDII scanner capable of reading all PCM codes. Common fixes: (1) Drain and refill DEF tank with fresh fluid (AutoZone DEF, Ford Motorcraft DEF VC-10-B) - $15-$30. (2) Replace DEF quality sensor ($150-$300). (3) Replace DEF injector ($300-$600 + labor). (4) SCR catalyst replacement ($2,000-$4,000). Always use fresh, quality-brand DEF (avoid bargain/store-brand DEF). Do not let DEF tank run to empty repeatedly.
symptoms: Check engine light with P207F (Reductant Quality Performance) code
Check engine light with P20EE (SCR NOx Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold)
Reduced engine power / limp mode
DEF gauge or warning light showing issue
Truck will not restart after excessive limp mode cycles
Rough running at idle
Increased fuel consumption

records.title: 6.7L Power Stroke EGR Cooler Clogging and Failure
records.description: The EGR (Exhaust Gas Recirculation) cooler on 2011-2019 6.7L Power Stroke diesel engines is prone to clogging with soot and eventually failing, particularly on trucks used for highway driving, light loads, or trucks that idle extensively. The EGR cooler recirculates cooled exhaust gas back into the intake to reduce NOx emissions. Over time, soot accumulates in the cooler's internal passages until coolant flow is restricted, causing the cooler to overheat and fail. When it fails, exhaust gases enter the coolant system, causing overheating and "puking" coolant from the degas bottle. The 2011-2014 models are particularly susceptible due to narrow internal coolant passages. Ford issued TSBs for 2011-2014 trucks covering EGR cooler cleaning/replacement under extended warranty up to 120,000 miles. The EGR cooler for 2011-2016 is OEM part BC3Z-9V425-A; 2017+ is HC3Z-9V425.
records.solution: Replace EGR cooler (BC3Z-9V425-A for 2011-2016; HC3Z-9V425 for 2017+). Check if truck qualifies for Ford extended service coverage with active DTC P0401 (Insufficient EGR Flow) or P2457 (EGR Cooler Performance). Some 2011-2014 trucks covered to 120,000 miles. Preventive: use a fuel additive (Diesel Kleen, Hot Shots Secret EDT) to reduce soot. Perform regular EGR cleaning at 60,000-mile intervals. Upgrade kits from Sinister Diesel and Dorman (904-405 kit) include both EGR cooler and gaskets.
symptoms: Coolant loss with no visible external leak
Coolant reservoir overflows or "pukes" coolant
White smoke from exhaust (coolant in combustion)
Engine overheating warning
DTC codes P0401 (Insufficient EGR Flow) or P2457 (EGR Cooler Performance)
Bubbling or foaming in coolant degas bottle
Loss of power under load (especially towing)
White deposits around degas bottle cap

records.title: 6.7L Power Stroke Early-Generation Turbocharger Failure (2011-2014)
records.description: The 2011-2014 6.7L Power Stroke uses a Honeywell DualBoost variable geometry turbocharger with ceramic bearings that proved unreliable in real-world use. The ceramic bearings fail prematurely, especially under hard towing use or when oil change intervals are stretched. The variable geometry turbo's complex actuator mechanism also sticks or fails. When the turbo fails, it is unmistakable: a deafening screeching sound accompanied by smoke from the tailpipe as the engine burns oil through the failed turbo seals. Ford recognized the early turbo design was problematic and switched to a single-compressor-wheel variable geometry turbocharger in 2015, which is significantly more reliable. Retrofit kits for 2011-2014 trucks are available.
records.solution: Replace turbocharger with updated 2015+ style single-compressor VGT unit using a retrofit kit (available from Drivingline/Banks Power aftermarket suppliers). OEM replacement of original DualBoost turbo is $2,500-$4,000 for the unit alone, plus 4-6 hours labor. Updated single-scroll VGT from 2015 is more reliable and kits allow installation on 2011-2014. Critical: always let turbocharged diesel idle for 3-5 minutes before shutdown to allow turbo bearing cooling.
symptoms: Loud, deafening screeching or wailing noise from engine compartment
Blue/black smoke from exhaust (oil burning through failed turbo seals)
Significant loss of power - engine goes into limp mode
Check engine light with turbocharger-related codes
Boost pressure too low codes (P0299)
Excessive oil consumption
Oil in intercooler or intake tract

records.title: 3.0L Vulcan Lower Intake Manifold Gasket / Coolant Tube Leak
records.description: The base 3.0L Vulcan V6 develops coolant leaks at the lower intake manifold gasket area and at a steel coolant crossover tube that is pressed into the aluminum manifold. The gasket hardens with age and the steel-into-aluminum tube joint corrodes and loosens, letting coolant seep externally or into the intake/cylinders. This is a slow age/heat-cycle failure that gradually worsens, and it is often confused with the front timing-cover gasket leak, which sits in the same area. Left unaddressed, coolant loss leads to overheating.
records.solution: Replace the lower intake manifold gaskets with updated gaskets and reseal the crossover tube; a common durable repair is to drill out the corroded steel tube and install a threaded (1/8 NPT) brass nipple/fitting. Inspect the timing-cover gasket at the same time since access overlaps, and flush/refill the cooling system.
symptoms: Visible coolant leak / drips at front of engine
Steady coolant loss from reservoir
Sweet coolant smell
Heater blowing cool air
Occasional overheating
Lean-bank trouble codes if vacuum leak develops

records.title: 3.8L Essex V6 Head Gasket Failure
records.description: The 3.8L 'Essex' V6 (an optional engine in 1990-1995 Taurus/Sable, distinct from the base 3.0 Vulcan) is notorious for premature head gasket failure. The aluminum heads expand and contract at a different rate than the cast-iron block, and the original composite head gasket cannot control the movement, letting combustion gases and coolant cross, typically failing between 60,000 and 100,000 miles. Ford issued TSB 98-4-9 acknowledging the defect on 1988-1995 3.8L FWD cars and released redesigned gaskets and head bolts; it later extended coverage via Campaign 98M01 and Service Campaign 00M09 (7yr/100k on some 1994-95 FWD models). If ignored, the resulting overheating can warp the aluminum heads or hydrolock the engine, turning a gasket job into an engine replacement.
records.solution: Replace both head gaskets with the updated Ford design (or an aftermarket MLS gasket) plus new torque-to-yield head bolts; have the heads checked for flatness and resurfaced if warped. A full cooling-system flush and pressure test should accompany the repair. Labor is 7-9 hours per Ford's TSB.
symptoms: Overheating
White exhaust smoke / sweet coolant smell
Coolant loss with no visible external leak
Milky oil or oil in coolant
Bubbling in the coolant reservoir
Rough idle or misfire after warm-up

records.title: Premature Alternator Failure
records.description: The 2000-2007 Ford Taurus experiences premature alternator failure, with some units failing as early as 34,000 miles according to Taurus Club of America forum reports. CarComplaints.com documents alternator failure as a reported issue for the 1997-2007 model years with an average repair cost of $270 at 135,750 miles. The 2002-2007 generation appears most affected based on forum complaint density. YourMechanic.com estimates alternator replacement between $533 and $695 for most Taurus model years. Symptoms include dashboard battery warning light, dimming headlights at idle, difficulty starting, and eventual complete electrical system failure and stalling. The internal voltage regulator is a common failure point, along with bearing wear that produces a grinding noise.
records.solution: Replace the alternator - the internal voltage regulator is not serviceable separately on Taurus alternators. OEM Motorcraft alternators are recommended over cheap rebuilt units that have high return rates. Cost is $533-695 at an independent shop per RepairPal/YourMechanic. When replacing, also inspect the serpentine belt and automatic belt tensioner - a worn tensioner can cause belt slippage that mimics alternator failure. Test the battery after alternator replacement - a chronically undercharged battery may have permanent sulfation damage.
symptoms: Battery warning light illuminated on dashboard
Dimming headlights, especially at idle
Difficulty starting or slow cranking
Vehicle stalls while driving (complete alternator failure)
Grinding or whining noise from alternator
Electrical accessories flickering or losing power
Battery drains overnight despite being new

records.title: AXOD-E / AX4S 4-Speed Automatic Transaxle Failure
records.description: The electronically controlled AXOD-E 4-speed automatic (renamed AX4S in 1993) has a poor reliability record on early-1990s Taurus/Sable, primarily due to inadequate internal lubrication: the final-drive assembly received only a constant ~5-7 psi, starving the geartrain so it overheats and self-destructs ('geartrain meltdown'). A 1995 Consumer Reports survey found nearly 20% of 1991 Taurus/Sable owners reported a serious transmission problem in a single year. Ford redesigned the filter-tube feed in mid-1992 and extended warranties on affected 1991 cars. Lubrication and capacity upgrades made when the unit became the AX4S in 1993 (and further improvements through 1995) helped, but these transaxles remain a known weak point across the decade.
records.solution: Rebuild or replace with an updated AX4S/AX4N unit incorporating the revised lubrication circuit and upgraded clutches. Ensure the cooler and lines are flushed to remove debris from the failed unit. Regular fluid/filter service (Mercon) and avoiding overheating (add-on cooler) extend life; erratic or harsh shifting should be diagnosed early before hard-part damage occurs.
symptoms: Slipping or delayed engagement
Harsh or erratic shifting
Hesitation or flare between gears
Overheating fluid / burnt smell
Sudden loss of drive
Stalling when coming to a stop

records.title: 3.5L Duratec Cam Phaser Rattle
records.description: The 3.5L Duratec V6 in later model Taurus vehicles develops cam phaser rattle on cold starts due to worn variable valve timing actuators and depleted oil control valve seals.
records.solution: Confirm the noise is coming from the front timing cover area during a cold start, then scan for VCT-related DTCs such as P0011, P0012, P0021, or P0022 and verify oil level/condition and oil pressure first, since dirty or low oil can aggravate phaser noise. The proper repair is to replace the worn cam phasers and VCT/OCV solenoids, and on higher-mileage engines it is wise to install new timing chains, guides, tensioners, and related seals/gaskets because the front cover must be removed to access the components. After reassembly, perform an oil and filter change with the correct viscosity oil, clear codes, and verify quiet cold-start operation; typical repair cost is about $1,500-$3,000 depending on whether only phasers/solenoids are replaced or a full timing set service is done.
symptoms: Rattling noise on cold start
Check engine light
Rough idle when cold

records.title: Ignition Switch Internal Short / Fire Risk (Recall 96V-071)
records.description: 1990-1993 Taurus (as part of a broad 1988-1993 Ford/Lincoln/Mercury population) were included in the April 1996 recall of ~7.9 million vehicles for an ignition switch defect (NHTSA 96V-071). A plastic barrier between the battery and ground terminals inside the switch can deteriorate and short internally, overheating even with the key off and the car parked. Ford received complaints of at least 1,100 fires in the U.S. and Canada, some igniting garages and homes. This is one of the largest fire-related recalls in NHTSA history.
records.solution: Have the ignition switch replaced under recall 96V-071 (Ford recall 96S28), free at a Ford dealer if not already performed. For vehicles where the recall was completed decades ago, verify the correct updated switch is installed; any switch that runs hot, causes intermittent stalling, or shows melted housing should be replaced immediately.
symptoms: Burning/electrical smell from steering column
Smoke from dash with key off
Vehicle fire while parked
Intermittent no-crank or stalling
Melted or discolored ignition switch housing

records.title: Power Steering Pump Failure and Fluid Leaks
records.description: The 1996-2007 Ford Taurus with hydraulic power steering (3.0L Vulcan and 3.0L Duratec V6 engines) is prone to power steering pump failure, often presenting as whining/groaning noises when turning, fluid leaks, and eventual complete loss of power assist. The Taurus Club of America forums document cases of sudden power steering loss that nearly caused accidents. RepairPal estimates replacement cost between $422 and $520 for most model years. The power steering pump bearings wear from heat and normal use, and the pump housing can develop internal leaks. The power steering hose connections are also prone to developing leaks at the high-pressure fitting. This issue is particularly common on Taurus models used for fleet/taxi service due to the increased steering load from constant low-speed maneuvering.
records.solution: Replace the power steering pump and flush the entire system with fresh Mercon V ATF (Ford specifies ATF, not generic power steering fluid, for Taurus). Also inspect the high-pressure hose and return hose for leaks - if the hose is leaking at the crimped fitting, the entire hose must be replaced. Pump replacement cost is $422-520 at an independent shop per RepairPal. For preventive maintenance, check power steering fluid level monthly and flush every 50,000 miles.
symptoms: Whining or groaning noise when turning the steering wheel
Steering becomes heavy or difficult, especially at low speeds
Power steering fluid puddle under vehicle
Power steering fluid level drops repeatedly
Squealing noise from engine bay when turning
Sudden complete loss of power steering assist
Steering wheel jerks or pulses during turns

records.title: Rear Subframe / Engine Cradle Corrosion (Salt-Belt Cars)
records.description: Third-generation (1996-1999) Taurus/Sable in road-salt regions are documented rusting through the rear subframe (engine cradle) and its mounting/carriage bolts. The subframe carries the engine and transaxle and anchors the lower control arms and steering; severe corrosion can let the cradle separate or drop, causing loss of steering control. Owners have reported rot-through at under 100,000 miles, in some cases on garage-kept cars. Ford declined warranty coverage for many owners, and NHTSA received multiple frame/member complaints for these years.
records.solution: Have the subframe and carriage bolts inspected by a shop familiar with the platform. Surface rust can be treated and undercoated; perforated or structurally compromised subframes must be replaced with a sound used or new cradle (a significant labor job because the powertrain must be supported and the cradle dropped). Prevention: annual undercarriage wash and undercoating in salt states.
symptoms: Visible heavy rust/perforation on rear subframe
Rusted or crumbling carriage/subframe bolts
Clunking or shifting powertrain over bumps
Vague or compromised steering
Sagging engine cradle

records.title: SHO V8 (Yamaha 3.4L) Camshaft Sprocket Failure
records.description: The 3.4L 60-degree V8 built by Yamaha for the 1996-1999 Taurus SHO uses camshaft sprockets that are 'swaged' (a metal ball forced through the hollow camshaft to press the sprocket on) rather than keyed or bolted. This joint can slip, letting the sprocket spin or 'walk' independently of the cam. Because the engine is an interference design, when the joint lets go the camshaft stops turning while the timing chain keeps moving, the valves stop actuating, and pistons strike valves, destroying the engine. Failures are commonly documented around 50,000 miles; roughly 1,200 of ~20,000 V8 SHOs (about 6%) are documented to have suffered it. Ford's only response was TSB 03-14-1 (Loctite application), widely regarded as inadequate; a replacement Yamaha long-block is scarce and costly, so a failure typically totals the car.
records.solution: Preventively pin or weld the cam sprockets to the camshafts before failure (the accepted community fix). If the engine has already grenaded, options are a rebuilt/pinned long-block or a used engine that has had the sprocket fix performed. There is no factory recall, this is an owner-borne repair.
symptoms: Sudden loss of power / engine stops running
Severe misfire or backfiring
Loud valvetrain noise before failure
Bent valves / no compression
Check engine light with cam/crank correlation codes

records.title: AX4S/AX4N Automatic Transmission Failure
records.description: The AX4S and later AX4N automatic transmissions used in the Taurus are prone to premature failure due to torque converter clutch issues, valve body wear, and overheating. Common in high-mileage vehicles and those used for frequent stop-and-go driving.
records.solution: Confirm the failure with a road test and scan for transmission-related DTCs, then inspect fluid condition/level and line pressure to determine whether the problem is a worn valve body, failing torque converter clutch, or internal clutch/band damage. Minor cases may be improved by replacing the EPC/shift solenoids, installing a valve body repair kit or updated valve body, servicing the filter, and adding/repairing an auxiliary transmission cooler to control heat; if the unit is slipping badly, shuddering in multiple gears, or has contaminated/burnt fluid, a full rebuild or quality remanufactured AX4S/AX4N with a new torque converter is the proper fix. Typical costs are about $400-$900 for valve body/solenoid repairs and fluid service, $150-$400 for cooler repairs or installation, and roughly $2,000-$3,500+ for a complete rebuild or replacement transmission.
symptoms: Harsh or delayed shifting
Slipping between gears
Transmission warning light
Shuddering during acceleration

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 98V288 - Taurus Transmission Cooler Line

records.title: 3.0L Vulcan V6 Head Gasket Failure
records.description: The 3.0L Vulcan V6 engine is susceptible to head gasket failure, often presenting as coolant mixing with oil or external coolant leaks. The composite head gaskets deteriorate over time, especially with overheating events.
records.solution: Confirm head gasket failure with a cooling-system pressure test, combustion-gas/block test, and compression or leak-down test, then inspect for coolant in the oil and external seepage at the head-to-block mating surface. Repair requires removing both cylinder heads, checking head and block deck flatness, machining the heads if needed, and installing new head gaskets with new torque-to-yield head bolts; it is also wise to replace the thermostat, water pump if suspect, and thoroughly flush contaminated oil and coolant. If the engine was severely overheated or bearing damage is present from coolant-contaminated oil, a complete engine replacement may be more cost-effective. Typical repair cost is about $1,500-$3,000 for head gasket service, or $3,000-$5,500 for a remanufactured engine installation.
symptoms: Coolant loss without visible leak
White exhaust smoke
Overheating
Milky oil on dipstick

records.title: ATX/AXOD Automatic Transaxle Premature Failure
records.description: The 3-speed ATX automatic transaxle used in the Ford Tempo is one of Ford's most failure-prone transmissions. The direct clutch and intermediate band fail prematurely, causing loss of 2nd gear or all forward gears. The governor valve sticks, causing delayed or no upshifts. The differential side gears also wear, creating a clicking noise in turns. Ford replaced the ATX with a 4-speed transaxle in some later models, but both units have reliability issues.
records.solution: Rebuilt transaxles with upgraded clutch packs are available for $800-1,200 from transmission rebuilders. A shift kit improves clutch apply firmness. Regular fluid changes (every 30,000 miles) with Mercon are essential for longevity. Many owners with manual transmission versions report far better reliability — consider a manual swap if the automatic fails.
symptoms: Loss of 2nd gear — engine revs but no acceleration in 2nd
No forward gears — reverse still works
Delayed engagement from Park to Drive (5+ seconds)
Clicking noise from transaxle in turns
Erratic shifting or failure to upshift

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 90E043001 - Ford Tempo Airbag Inflator

records.title: Heater Core Leak and Coolant Smell
records.description: The heater core is prone to developing leaks, causing a sweet coolant smell inside the cabin, fogging on the windshield, and wet carpet on the passenger side. The dash must be partially disassembled for replacement.
records.solution: Replace the heater core. Flush the cooling system and replace coolant. Check for corrosion in heater hoses as well.
symptoms: Sweet smell inside cabin
Windshield fogs up
Wet passenger floor
Coolant level drops

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 97V019 - Tempo Cooling-Fan Snow Intrusion

records.title: 2.3L HSC Head Gasket Failure
records.description: The 2.3L High Swirl Combustion (HSC) 4-cylinder in the Ford Tempo is well known for premature head gasket failure, often before 100,000 miles. The iron block and head expand at similar rates but the original composite head gasket material deteriorates from coolant chemistry. The head gasket fails between cylinders 2 and 3 most commonly, causing a compression leak that produces a rough idle and misfires. External coolant leaks at the rear of the head are also common.
records.solution: Replace the head gasket with a Fel-Pro multi-layer steel replacement. Have the cylinder head resurfaced and checked for cracks. Replace the head bolts (reusable but often stretched). Replace the thermostat and flush the cooling system. This is a straightforward repair on the 2.3L HSC — the head is easily accessible.
symptoms: Coolant level dropping slowly
White smoke from exhaust at startup
Rough idle and misfires on cylinders 2 and 3
Engine overheating in traffic
Coolant visible leaking at rear of head/block mating surface

records.title: Ignition Module Failure
records.description: The TFI (Thick Film Ignition) module mounted on the distributor is prone to heat-related failure, causing intermittent stalling and no-start conditions. The module's location on the distributor exposes it to excessive engine heat.
records.solution: Relocate the TFI module away from the distributor using a remote mount kit, or replace with an updated module. Adding heat sink compound improves longevity.
symptoms: Intermittent stalling
No-start when engine is hot
Engine cuts out at highway speed
Restarts after cooling down

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 96V071 - Ford Tempo Ignition Switch

records.title: Front Lower Control Arm Bushing Deterioration
records.description: The Ford Tempo front suspension uses lower control arms with rubber bushings that deteriorate rapidly, especially in northern climates with road salt. The bushings crack and separate from the metal sleeve, allowing excessive control arm movement. This causes vague steering, poor handling, and accelerated tire wear. The Tempo's MacPherson strut suspension is sensitive to control arm bushing condition.
records.solution: Replace both lower control arms with new units — the bushings are not separately serviceable and the arms are inexpensive ($40-60 each). Replace strut mounts and sway bar end links at the same time as they typically wear at a similar rate. A front-end alignment is required after replacement.
symptoms: Clunking from front end over bumps
Vague or wandering steering
Inner edge tire wear on front tires
Vehicle pulls to one side under braking
Steering wheel vibration at highway speeds

records.title: Retro Thunderbird Convertible Top and Hardtop Water Leaks
records.description: The 2002-2005 retro Thunderbird's removable hardtop and convertible soft top develop water leaks at the window seals and header weatherstripping. Water enters the cabin during rain and car washes, pooling in the footwells and damaging electronics.
records.solution: Replace the header seal weatherstripping and window run channel seals. Apply weatherstrip adhesive where seals have pulled away. For the hardtop, realign the locating pins and check the rear seal compression.
symptoms: Water dripping in cabin during rain
Wet carpet in footwells
Water stains on headliner edges
Musty smell inside
Water visible at windshield header
Damp seats after car wash

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 02V169 - 2002 Thunderbird Driver Seat Belt

records.title: 3.8L V6 Head Gasket Failure
records.description: The naturally aspirated 3.8L Essex V6 Thunderbird shares the same head gasket vulnerability as the Windstar and Mustang. The composite gaskets fail between coolant passages and cylinders.
symptoms: White exhaust smoke
Coolant loss
Overheating
Rough idle

records.title: Convertible Top Hydraulic System Failure
records.description: The hydraulic system for the power convertible top develops leaks in the cylinders, lines, or pump. The top may stop mid-cycle or refuse to operate. Hydraulic fluid leaks onto the trunk area.
records.solution: Inspect hydraulic lines, cylinders, and the pump for leaks. Replace failed components. The hydraulic fluid is specific to the system — use only the recommended type. Bleed the system after repairs.
symptoms: Top stops mid-cycle
Slow top operation
Hydraulic fluid leak in trunk
Top warning light

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 04V330 - Thunderbird Power Seat Support

records.title: Super Coupe Supercharger and Intercooler Failure
records.description: The 3.8L V6 Super Coupe uses an Eaton M90 supercharger that develops boost leaks, bearing noise, and coupler failure over time. The intercooler system can also develop leaks, reducing boost efficiency.
records.solution: Diagnose the Super Coupe’s Eaton M90 by checking for rotor shaft play, nose drive bearing noise, and a worn coupler, then pressure-test the intake tract and intercooler for boost leaks at the supercharger outlet, intercooler core, and connecting hoses. Repair typically involves rebuilding the supercharger nose with new bearings and coupler or replacing the unit entirely, along with replacing cracked vacuum/boost hoses, intercooler seals, or a leaking intercooler core. Verify boost with a road test and confirm proper supercharger oil level and condition after repair. Typical costs range from about $150-$400 for a coupler/nose rebuild, $600-$1,200 for a rebuilt supercharger, and $200-$600 more if intercooler components or hoses also need replacement.
symptoms: Whining or grinding from supercharger
Loss of boost
Reduced power
Boost gauge reads low

records.title: Side Window Regulator Failure
records.description: The frameless door window regulators fail, causing the windows to drop into the door or bind when raising. The windows must seal tightly since there is no door frame, making this a security and weather issue.
records.solution: Replace the window regulator assembly. Lubricate the window channel with silicone spray. Adjust window alignment to ensure proper seal when closed.
symptoms: Window drops into door
Slow window operation
Window doesn't seal at top
Wind noise when closed

records.title: 10R80 (10-speed) Harsh/Delayed Shifts and Shudder (Software/Valve Body Related)
records.description: Later Transits equipped with the 10R80 10-speed automatic have documented owner complaints of harsh 1-2/2-3 shifts, delayed engagement, and occasional shudder. Ford has issued multiple service communications/TSBs across Ford platforms using the 10R80 addressing shift quality via PCM/TCM calibration updates and, in some cases, valve body service. Drivers often describe banging into gear, flare, or hesitation when pulling into traffic.
records.solution: Perform the latest PCM/TCM calibration update per Ford service publications; if symptoms persist, diagnose for valve body issues and solenoid performance and service/replace the main control/valve body as directed. Verify fluid level/condition using the correct MERCON ULV specification and follow Ford fill procedure.
symptoms: Harsh upshift or downshift (bang/jerk)
Delayed engagement into Drive/Reverse
Shudder at light throttle
Shift flare or hesitation between gears
Intermittent transmission fault messages

citations.title: Ford TSB 24-2254 - 10R80 Harsh or Delayed Engagement and Shift

records.title: 3.7L Ti-VCT Throttle Body Failure / Electronic Throttle Control (ETC) Limp Mode
records.description: Owners report sudden loss of power with a wrench light and reduced throttle response, often while cruising or accelerating. NHTSA complaints and Ford service information describe electronic throttle body internal faults (TPS/actuator) that can trigger ETC failsafe and limp mode on 3.7L Ti-VCT Transits. The condition may be intermittent at first and then become frequent, especially with heat/soak and higher mileage.
records.solution: Replace the electronic throttle body assembly and perform throttle/PCM relearn. Common service fix is throttle body replacement (Ford throttle body assembly; part number varies by year/engine calibration) and inspection/cleaning of throttle connector pins and harness strain relief.
symptoms: Wrench light / 'See Manual' message
Sudden reduced power / limp mode
Poor throttle response or no acceleration
Rough idle or stalling when coming to a stop
Intermittent ETC-related DTCs

records.title: 3.5L EcoBoost First-Gen Timing Chain Stretch and Rattle
records.description: The first-generation 3.5L EcoBoost (2011-2016) used in the 2015-2017 Ford Transit 350/350 HD with the twin-turbocharged V6 is known for premature timing chain stretch. The single-chain-per-bank design (two chains total) stretches as the links wear individually, causing the chain to effectively grow longer. A stretched chain causes VCT timing correlation codes, cold-start rattling, rough idle, and eventual jumped timing. Ford revised the 3.5L EcoBoost design in 2017 to use dual chains per bank (four total), which substantially resolved the stretch issue. Transit vans used for commercial/fleet service with high-idle hours accumulate chain wear faster than typical passenger vehicles. The F150 EcoBoost Forum documents thousands of cases of this specific 3.5L chain issue and contains multiple long-running troubleshooting threads.
records.solution: Complete timing chain replacement required: both primary chains, all guides, and tensioners must be replaced simultaneously. In 2017+, Ford redesigned to dual-chain design which resolved the issue. Remanufactured short block or long block replacement is an option for high-mileage engines if chain guides have also failed. Use only 5W-30 full synthetic and change every 5,000-7,500 miles. Labor: 10-14 hours on Transit due to engine mount complexity.
symptoms: Cold-start rattle from engine (first 2-5 seconds on startup)
Check engine light with P0016, P0017, P0020, P0021 (cam-crank timing correlation)
Rough idle, especially when cold
Poor fuel economy
Engine hesitation or stumble
Loss of power under acceleration
Drivability issues that worsen over time

records.title: 3.5L EcoBoost Twin Turbocharger Failure
records.description: The Ford Transit 350/350 HD with the 3.5L EcoBoost twin-turbocharged V6 experiences turbocharger failures from inadequate lubrication, carbon buildup in the turbo housings, wastegate actuator failure, and turbo bearing wear. OMS AutoParts and Autodoc document common Transit turbo problems including loss of power, turbo lag, unusual whistling/whining/grinding noises, and excessive smoke. The commercial use of Transit vans (frequent stop-and-go, high idle hours, heavy loads) accelerates turbo wear beyond what passenger vehicle applications typically experience. FordTransitUSAForum.com documents a case of turbo and manifold failure at 38,000 miles on a 3.5L EcoBoost Transit 350. RepairPal estimates turbocharger assembly replacement between $1,650 and $2,210 depending on the Transit model variant.
records.solution: For wastegate actuator failures (most common turbo issue): replacement of the actuator alone ($200-400) may resolve boost control issues without full turbo replacement. For internal turbo bearing failure or impeller damage, complete turbo replacement is required. RepairPal estimates $1,650-2,210 for turbo assembly replacement. For Transit commercial vehicles, change oil every 5,000 miles (not the factory 10k interval) and allow 30-60 seconds of idle time before shutdown after sustained driving to allow turbo bearing oil to circulate. Never shut off a hot turbocharged engine immediately after towing or hard driving.
symptoms: Loss of power or reduced boost
Excessive turbo lag (slow boost response)
Whistling, whining, or grinding noise from turbo area
Excessive blue or black smoke from exhaust
Check engine light with boost-related codes
Oil leak from turbo drain or feed lines
Burning oil smell from engine bay
Reduced fuel economy

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 14V482 - Transit Rear Brake Hoses

records.title: 6R80 Transmission Torque Converter Shudder at Light Throttle
records.description: Ford Transit models equipped with the 6R80 6-speed automatic transmission are prone to a torque converter clutch (TCC) shudder felt as a vibration or flutter between approximately 40–55 mph during light throttle cruise conditions. The issue is caused by degradation of the transmission fluid's friction modifier additives, which are necessary for smooth TCC lockup engagement on the Ford-spec Mercon LV fluid. Ford issued TSB 16-0094 specifically addressing this shudder condition on the Transit and other Mercon LV-equipped vehicles.
records.solution: Perform a complete transmission fluid drain and refill using fresh Ford Mercon LV fluid (Motorcraft XT-10-QLVC). Ford TSB 16-0094 recommends this as the first step. In persistent cases, a friction modifier additive (Ford Motorcraft Friction Modifier XT-11-QDC) can be added. If shudder persists after fluid service, torque converter replacement may be required.
symptoms: Vibration or shudder felt through the vehicle body at 40–55 mph
Condition occurs specifically during light throttle cruise, not acceleration
Shudder disappears when accelerating or coasting
Symptom worsens as transmission fluid degrades with mileage
No fault codes typically stored (perceived as road vibration by owners)

records.title: Alternator Premature Failure and Voltage Regulator Issues
records.description: Ford Transit vans experience premature alternator failure, often between 50,000-80,000 miles. The internal voltage regulator fails first, causing undercharging or overcharging conditions. Commercial Transit vans with aftermarket upfitter packages (extra lighting, inverters, refrigeration units) are particularly susceptible due to sustained high electrical loads. Symptoms often start as intermittent battery warnings before progressing to a no-start condition.
records.solution: Replace the alternator assembly with a high-output unit (250A) if the vehicle has aftermarket electrical loads, or OEM replacement (220A) for stock configurations. Always replace the serpentine belt and tensioner at the same time. Test the battery — a failing battery can cause alternator overwork and premature failure. For vans with upfitter packages, install a dual-battery isolator system to prevent alternator overload.
symptoms: Battery warning light illuminated
Dimming headlights or interior lights
Electrical accessories cutting out intermittently
Battery repeatedly dying overnight
Whining noise from alternator area that changes with RPM
Voltage gauge reading below 13.5V or above 15V

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 18V275 - Expanded Transit Trailer-Tow Module Population

records.title: Body Control Module (BCM) Failure Causing Intermittent Electrical Gremlins
records.description: Ford Transit BCMs, particularly on 2015–2019 models, have been reported to fail or develop software faults causing a wide array of seemingly unrelated electrical issues including random door lock cycling, instrument cluster malfunctions, and accessory power loss. Water intrusion from sunroof drains or cowl leaks can accelerate BCM failure by corroding the module's internal connectors. Ford TSB 18-2175 acknowledged BCM programming faults contributing to some of these behaviors.
records.solution: Diagnose with Ford IDS/FDRS scan tool to identify BCM fault codes. If water intrusion is present, address the leak source first. BCM replacement (Ford part number varies by configuration, ~$300–$500 OEM) and programming/configuration to the vehicle using Ford PATS and IDS is required. In some cases, a BCM software update alone resolves the issue.
symptoms: Random door locks cycling or activating on their own
Instrument cluster warning lights illuminating without cause
Power windows or accessories becoming inoperative intermittently
Battery drain or parasitic draw
Multiple unrelated fault codes stored across modules

records.title: Brake Vacuum Pump Oil Leak / Reduced Brake Assist (3.5L EcoBoost & 3.7L)
records.description: Owner complaints and service reports document vacuum pump oil leaks that can reduce available brake assist and/or create oil seepage on the engine. The mechanical vacuum pump seals can leak, and in some cases vacuum output drops, leading to a harder brake pedal especially after repeated stops. This is most often reported on gasoline Transits using an engine-driven vacuum pump for brake booster assist.
records.solution: Test vacuum output and inspect for oil leakage at the vacuum pump and gasket. Replace the vacuum pump and seal/gasket as needed, clean contaminated areas, and verify brake booster operation and vacuum reserve after repair.
symptoms: Hard brake pedal / reduced brake assist
Oil leak near vacuum pump area
Hissing/vacuum noise
Longer stopping distance feel
Brake warning messages in some cases

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 26V090 - Transit Brake Pedal and Booster Pushrod

records.title: A/C Compressor Failure or No-Cool Condition (Refrigerant Leak/Compressor Damage)
records.description: Owners report loss of A/C cooling, compressor noise, or compressor clutch/variable displacement control issues leading to warm air. Some cases involve refrigerant leaks at seals/lines, while others involve compressor internal failure contaminating the system. Transit Connect owner reports and service documentation frequently cite compressor replacement and system flush as the corrective action.
records.solution: Recover and measure refrigerant, leak-test with dye/nitrogen, and repair leaking components (O-rings/lines/condenser as needed). If compressor has failed internally, replace the compressor, receiver/drier (or desiccant), and expansion device as applicable, then flush lines and evacuate/recharge to spec.
symptoms: A/C blows warm or intermittently cool
Compressor noise (grinding/rattling)
A/C cycles rapidly
Low-side pressure abnormal
Refrigerant oil/dye residue at fittings

records.title: ABS Wheel Speed Sensor/Wiring Fault (ABS/Traction Control Lights On)
records.description: Transit Connect owners report intermittent ABS and traction control warnings caused by wheel speed sensor signal dropouts, often due to sensor contamination, corrosion at connectors, or damaged wiring near the hubs. The issue can be intermittent and may also disable stability control functions until repaired. This pattern appears in NHTSA complaints and owner reports describing ABS/AdvanceTrac warnings and sensor replacement.
records.solution: Scan ABS module for wheel speed sensor DTCs and view live wheel speed data to identify the affected corner. Clean/inspect tone rings (if applicable), repair wiring/connectors, or replace the wheel speed sensor; clear codes and verify on a road test.
symptoms: ABS warning light illuminated
Traction control/AdvanceTrac warning
ABS activates unexpectedly at low speed (sometimes)
Speedometer fluctuation (rare)
Stored wheel speed sensor DTCs

records.title: Brake Vacuum Pump Leak/Failure (Hard Brake Pedal, Reduced Assist)
records.description: Some Transit Connect owners report a hard brake pedal and reduced brake assist due to vacuum pump leakage or failure on engines using a mechanical vacuum pump for brake boost. Oil seepage at the pump and declining vacuum can lead to increased stopping effort, especially at low RPM. This condition is documented in owner reports and service information addressing vacuum pump performance and leaks on Ford applications used in Transit Connect powertrains.
records.solution: Measure vacuum supply under load and inspect for oil leaks at the vacuum pump and hose connections; replace the vacuum pump and any contaminated hoses/check valves as needed. After repair, verify brake assist and confirm no vacuum leaks remain.
symptoms: Hard brake pedal
Longer stopping distance due to reduced assist
Hissing/vacuum leak noise near pump
Oil seepage around vacuum pump area
Brake assist worse at idle/low RPM
